claims.text: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is a eutectic alloy containing coupled FCC and B2 phases.
The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy has a fine lamellar microstructure.
The as-cast alloy exhibits high ductility.
The initial high ductility is caused by coherent phase boundaries and a relatively disordered B2 phase.
Intermediate aging, exemplified by 400–600 °C, causes a transient loss of ductility.
Aging at higher temperatures restores ductility after the intermediate-temperature embrittlement.
Intermediate aging increases local chemical order, chemical short-range order, and long-range B2 ordering within the B2 phase.
Increased chemical ordering raises the critical resolved shear stress or Peierls barrier for dislocation glide in B2.
The increased glide barrier suppresses cross-slip and favors planar dislocation slip.
Planar slip in ordered B2 domains produces localized stress concentrations at FCC/B2 interfaces.
Aging changes the FCC/B2 phase boundaries from coherent or semi-coherent to incoherent.
Ordering-induced lattice-parameter mismatch and interfacial segregation of ordering elements cause the loss of phase-boundary coherency.
Incoherent phase boundaries impede dislocation transmission between FCC and B2.
Planar slip combined with impeded phase-boundary transmission causes localized stress and brittle fracture.
At higher temperatures, thermal activation of cross-slip contributes to ductility recovery.
Disordering or coarsening of ordered domains at higher temperatures reduces planar slip and restores strain delocalization.
The lower boundary of the embrittlement regime occurs where LCO formation and phase-boundary coherency loss become sufficient.
The upper boundary occurs when LCO disordering or domain coarsening restores cross-slip and phase-boundary coherency.
The transition is driven by LCO and phase-boundary evolution rather than impurity-driven grain-boundary embrittlement.
Dislocations and microbands can cross FCC/B2 interfaces, and such transmission contributes to synergistic, uniform deformation.
